1| # Browser integration
2| 
3| This is the **companion surface** for browser runtimes. See [Runtime Surfaces](./surfaces.md).
4| 
5| Browser apps cannot run the full agentic surface (tool execution, LSP, MCP, workflows, daemon HTTP). Those require Bun. This guide is the shared foundation for every browser entrypoint: auth, transport, realtime events, error handling, and observability. For web-UI-application patterns built on this foundation, entrypoint selection, companion chat, attachments, and voice playback, see [Web UI integration](./web-ui-integration.md).
6| 
7| Use `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser` when a browser app needs the complete
8| operator route contract. Use scoped browser entrypoints when an app owns one
9| extension surface:
10| 
11| - `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/knowledge` for the base knowledge/wiki WebUI.
12| - `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/homeassistant` for Home Assistant panels.
13| - `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/agent` (`createBrowserAgentPlatform`) for the GoodVibes Agent surface: the agent's own knowledge/wiki space under `/api/goodvibes-agent/knowledge`, plus work-plan, artifact, and companion-chat routes.
14| 
15| ```ts
16| import { createBrowserGoodVibesPlatform } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser';
17| 
18| const platformClient = createBrowserGoodVibesPlatform({
19|   baseUrl: 'https://goodvibes.example.com',
20| });
21| ```
22| 
23| Scoped entrypoints expose the same auth/token options and shared session routes
24| without loading unrelated route metadata:
25| 
26| ```ts
27| import { createBrowserKnowledgePlatform } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/knowledge';
28| 
29| const platformClient = createBrowserKnowledgePlatform({
30|   baseUrl: 'https://goodvibes.example.com',
31| });
32| 
33| await platformClient.knowledge.status();
34| ```
35| 
36| ## Auth
37| 
38| Preferred browser auth modes:
39| - same-origin cookie session
40| - bearer token when operating cross-origin or inside a custom shell
41| 
42| The HTTP transport always uses `credentials: 'include'`, so same-origin cookie-backed sessions work without additional wiring.
43| 
44| If you are using bearer tokens in the browser, pair the platform with `createBrowserTokenStore()` or your own `tokenStore` implementation.
45| 
46| ## Realtime
47| 
48| For browser UIs:
49| - use `platformClient.realtime.viaSse()` for operator dashboards and status views
50| - use `platformClient.realtime.viaWebSocket()` when you need a persistent duplex connection model
51| 
52| The browser entrypoint also enables conservative defaults for:
53| - HTTP retry on safe/idempotent requests
54| - SSE reconnect
55| - WebSocket reconnect
56| 
57| ## Example
58| 
59| ```ts
60| const events = platformClient.realtime.viaSse();
61| const unsubscribe = events.agents.on('AGENT_COMPLETED', (event) => {
62|   console.log(event);
63| });
64| ```
65| 
66| ## Same-origin recommendation
67| 
68| If the web UI is hosted with the daemon:
69| - prefer same-origin routing
70| - prefer cookie-backed session auth
71| - use SSE for live operator dashboards
72| 
73| If the app is cross-origin:
74| - use bearer tokens
75| - validate CORS explicitly
76| - prefer WebSocket if the deployment path is hostile to SSE
77| 
78| ## Error handling
79| 
80| All platform errors extend `GoodVibesError`. See [Error Kinds](./error-kinds.md) for the full taxonomy.
81| 
82| ```ts
83| import { GoodVibesError } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/errors';
84| 
85| try {
86|   await platformClient.operator.control.snapshot();
87| } catch (err) {
88|   if (err instanceof GoodVibesError) {
89|     switch (err.kind) {
90|       case 'auth':
91|         // session expired, redirect to login or refresh token
92|         break;
93|       case 'network':
94|         // transport failure, reconnect SSE/WS or retry
95|         break;
96|       case 'service':
97|         // daemon or upstream service returned 5xx, log and degrade gracefully
98|         break;
99|       case 'protocol':
100|         // client and daemon disagreed about the wire contract
101|         break;
102|       default:
103|         throw err;
104|     }
105|   }
106| }
107| ```
108| 
109| ## Observability
110| 
111| `PlatformObserver` is the right mechanism for dev-time logging in browser consoles. `createConsoleObserver()` logs auth transitions (`console.log`) and errors (`console.error`) by default; pass `createConsoleObserver({ level: 'debug' })` to also trace transport activity and every runtime event via `console.debug`. See [Observability](./observability.md) for the full observer API.
112| 
113| ```ts
114| import { createConsoleObserver } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/observer';
115| 
116| const platformClient = createBrowserGoodVibesPlatform({
117|   baseUrl: 'https://goodvibes.example.com',
118|   observer: createConsoleObserver({ level: 'debug' }),
119| });
120| ```
121|

state.text:
1| # platform error kinds
2| 
3| > Consumer reference. For handling patterns see [Error Handling](./error-handling.md); for internals see [Error Architecture](./errors.md).
4| 
5| Every error thrown by the platform's public surface is an instance of `GoodVibesError`. The `kind` field is the primary discriminant. Use it in `switch` statements or `if` chains instead of parsing `message` strings or using `instanceof` on subclasses.
6| 
7| ## Quick reference
8| 
9| | `kind` | Description | Retryable |
10| |--------|-------------|----------|
11| | `auth` | Credential or permission failure | No |
12| | `config` | Local platform misconfiguration | No |
13| | `contract` | Method/route contract violation | No |
14| | `network` | Transport or connectivity failure | Yes |
15| | `not-found` | Remote resource does not exist | No |
16| | `rate-limit` | Upstream rate limit exceeded | Yes |
17| | `protocol` | Wire-format or protocol failure | Sometimes |
18| | `service` | Upstream service or HTTP 5xx failure | Sometimes |
19| | `internal` | Daemon/internal platform failure | No |
20| | `tool` | Tool execution failure | Sometimes |
21| | `validation` | Input failed schema or value checks | No |
22| | `unknown` | Unclassified error | No |
23| 
24| ## Kinds in detail
25| 
26| ### `auth`
27| 
28| **When it fires:** The request was rejected due to authentication or authorization failure. Covers HTTP 401 (missing/invalid credentials), 402 (billing), and 403 (insufficient scopes).
29| 
30| **Remediation:**
31| - On 401: refresh the auth token or redirect to login.
32| - On 403: check the required scopes in `err.hint`; the user may need elevated permissions.
33| 
34| **Retryable:** No. Fix the credential situation first.
35| 
36| **Example `category` values:** `authentication`, `authorization`, `billing`, `permission`
37| 
38| ---
39| 
40| ### `config`
41| 
42| **When it fires:** The platform was called with a missing or invalid configuration value. For example, the HTTP transport's base-URL normalization throws this when `baseUrl` is empty (`ENGINE_TRANSPORT_BASE_URL_REQUIRED`) or is not a parseable absolute URL (`ENGINE_TRANSPORT_BASE_URL_INVALID`).
43| 
44| **Remediation:** Inspect `err.message` and `err.code` to identify the missing field, then fix the platform initialization options before retrying.
45| 
46| **Retryable:** No.
47| 
48| **Example `code` values:** `ENGINE_CONFIGURATION_ERROR`, `ENGINE_TRANSPORT_BASE_URL_REQUIRED`, `ENGINE_TRANSPORT_BASE_URL_INVALID`
49| 
50| ---
51| 
52| ### `contract`
53| 
54| **When it fires:** A method was invoked that has no registered HTTP binding, or a route ID was requested that does not exist in the contract manifest. These represent usage errors. The caller is invoking something the contract does not define.
55| 
56| **Remediation:** Verify the method ID or route ID against the operator contract manifest. This is typically a programming error caught at development time.
57| 
58| **Retryable:** No.
59| 
60| **Example `code` values:** `ENGINE_CONTRACT_ERROR`
61| 
62| ---
63| 
64| ### `network`
65| 
66| **When it fires:** The HTTP fetch failed before a response was received (DNS failure, connection refused, SSE stream error, transport timeout).
67| 
68| **Remediation:** Check connectivity and retry with exponential backoff. The platform's built-in retry policy (`DEFAULT_HTTP_RETRY_POLICY`) handles common transient cases automatically.
69| 
70| **Retryable:** Yes. `err.recoverable` will be `true`.
71| 
72| **Example `category` values:** `network`, `timeout`
73| 
74| ---
75| 
76| ### `not-found`
77| 
78| **When it fires:** The remote server returned HTTP 404.
79| 
80| **Remediation:** The resource does not exist at the server. Verify identifiers and do not retry.
81| 
82| **Retryable:** No.
83| 
84| ---
85| 
86| ### `rate-limit`
87| 
88| **When it fires:** The remote server returned HTTP 429.
89| 
90| **Remediation:** Wait for `err.retryAfterMs` milliseconds (if present) or use exponential backoff, then retry. The platform's retry policy handles this automatically.
91| 
92| **Retryable:** Yes. `err.recoverable` will be `true`.
93| 
94| ---
95| 
96| ### `protocol`
97| 
98| **When it fires:** The daemon or transport detected a wire-format, stream, contract framing, or protocol-level failure after a request reached the target.
99| 
100| **Remediation:** Check server/client version alignment and transport logs. Retry only when the operation is idempotent and `err.recoverable` is true.
101| 
102| **Retryable:** Sometimes. Check `err.recoverable`.
103| 
104| ---
105| 
106| ### `service`
107| 
108| **When it fires:** The remote service returned HTTP 5xx, or a daemon error body surfaced category `service`.
109| 
110| **Remediation:** Log `err.requestId` for debugging. Retry with backoff for 500/502/503/504, these are typically transient. Do not retry on 501.
111| 
112| **Retryable:** Sometimes. Check `err.recoverable`. The platform sets it based on status code. HTTP 500/502/503/504 are retryable by default.
113| 
114| ---
115| 
116| ### `internal`
117| 
118| **When it fires:** The daemon or platform surfaced a bug or invariant violation from inside GoodVibes rather than from user input, transport, or an upstream provider.
119| 
120| **Remediation:** Log the full structured error and report the bug. Do not rely on retry unless `err.recoverable` is explicitly true.
121| 
122| **Retryable:** No by default.
123| 
124| ---
125| 
126| ### `tool`
127| 
128| **When it fires:** Tool execution failed after dispatch, including tool runtime errors and tool-specific rejected operations.
129| 
130| **Remediation:** Inspect `err.category`, `err.message`, and the tool-specific trace. Retry only when the tool operation is idempotent and marked recoverable.
131| 
132| **Retryable:** Sometimes. Check `err.recoverable`.
133| 
134| ---
135| 
136| ### `validation`
137| 
138| **When it fires:** Input passed to a daemon route handler failed a required-field check or schema validation. For example, a schedule definition with an invalid or missing field.
139| 
140| **Remediation:** Fix the input payload. `err.message` describes which field or constraint failed.
141| 
142| **Retryable:** No.
143| 
144| **Example `category` values:** `bad_request`
145| 
146| ---
147| 
148| ### `unknown`
149| 
150| **When it fires:** The error could not be mapped to a specific kind. This is a catch-all for unexpected conditions that do not expose structured category metadata.
151| 
152| **Remediation:** Log the full error including `err.message`, `err.category`, and `err.requestId` for investigation.
153| 
154| **Retryable:** No (conservative default).
155| 
156| ---
157| 
158| ## Route-level error codes
159| 
160| Daemon HTTP routes return structured error bodies with a `code` string that is separate from the platform-layer `kind` discriminant. These codes appear in route-specific error responses and are not `GoodVibesError` instances. They are HTTP error body fields returned by the daemon before the platform maps them to a `GoodVibesError`.
161| 
162| Route-level codes are not standardized across the daemon. Different routes emit different strings for the same HTTP status, and some 401 responses omit a `code` field entirely (a bare `{ error: 'Unauthorized' }`). Treat this as a sample of codes actually in use, not an exhaustive or normalized catalog:
163| 
164| | Code | HTTP Status | Meaning |
165| |------|-------------|----------|
166| | `INVALID_KIND` | 400 | The `kind` field in a shared-session message body is not `task`, `message`, or `followup`. |
167| | `INVALID_REQUEST` | 400 | The request body failed a required-field or schema check. |
168| | `PROVIDER_NOT_CONFIGURED` | 409 | The requested media (voice/TTS) provider is not registered with the daemon's provider registry. |
169| | `AUTH_REQUIRED` | 401 | No valid bearer token or session cookie was present. Some routes return this code; others return a bare `{ error: 'Unauthorized' }` with no `code` field at all. |
170| | `MISSING_SCOPE` | 403 | The caller's principal authenticated but lacks the scope the route requires. |
171| | `NOT_FOUND` | 404 | The resource (session, artifact, job, etc.) does not exist. |
172| | `RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | The request was rejected by an upstream rate-limit policy. |
173| | `INTERNAL_ERROR` | 500 | The daemon encountered an unhandled internal error. |
174| 
175| The platform maps these HTTP error responses to `GoodVibesError` instances using the `kind` mapping above. To inspect the raw route-level code, read `err.code` on the thrown `GoodVibesError`. To cross-reference route-specific codes, check the route documentation for that namespace (e.g., [Companion Message Routing](./companion-message-routing.md) for `INVALID_KIND`).
176|

177| > **Three overlapping `code` value-spaces:** `err.code` is a single `string` field, but the value you read may come from any of three overlapping spaces:
178| >
179| > 1. **Canonical `EngineErrorCode`.** Codes the platform assigns to `GoodVibesError` (e.g. `RATE_LIMITED`, `AUTH_REQUIRED`, `PROTOCOL_ERROR`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`); see [Canonical platform error codes](#canonical-platform-error-codes).
180| > 2. **Daemon route-body codes.** Raw `code` strings in daemon HTTP error bodies (e.g. `INVALID_KIND`, `PROVIDER_NOT_CONFIGURED`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`, enumerated above) before the platform normalises them.
181| > 3. **`AppError`-subclass codes.** Literal codes declared by `AppError` subclasses (e.g. `CONFIG_ERROR`, `PROVIDER_ERROR`, `TOOL_ERROR`, `ACP_ERROR`, `PERMISSION_DENIED`, `RENDER_ERROR`); see [Config errors and the AppError hierarchy](#config-errors-and-the-apperror-hierarchy).
182| >
183| > There is **no suffix rule** distinguishing these spaces: `INTERNAL_ERROR` appears as both a route-body code and a canonical code, and subclass codes exist both with (`CONFIG_ERROR`) and without (`PERMISSION_DENIED`) the `_ERROR` suffix. Always switch on `err.kind` (the `EngineErrorKind` discriminant) first, then read `err.code` only to disambiguate further.
184| 
185| ---
186| 
187| ## Canonical platform error codes
188| 
189| Beyond the `kind` discriminant, every `GoodVibesError` carries a `code`. platform-produced errors set one of the canonical values in the `EngineErrorCode` union; caller-supplied codes may be any string, since `code` is typed `EngineErrorCode | (string & {})`.
190| 
191| Prefer the `EngineErrorCodes` const and the runtime guards over bare string literals:
192| 
193| - `isErrorCode(err, EngineErrorCodes.RATE_LIMITED)` returns `true` and narrows `err.code` to the given literal. It works on any object with an optional `code` field.
194| - `isKnownErrorCode(value)` returns `true` when an arbitrary string is one of the canonical codes, useful for values received over the wire.
195| 
196| ```ts
197| import { isErrorCode, EngineErrorCodes, GoodVibesError } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/errors';
198| 
199| try {
200|   await platformClient.operator.accounts.snapshot();
201| } catch (err) {
202|   if (err instanceof GoodVibesError && isErrorCode(err, EngineErrorCodes.RATE_LIMITED)) {
203|     await delay(err.retryAfterMs ?? 1000);
204|   }
205| }
206| ```
207| 
208| The full set of canonical codes, available as `EngineErrorCodes.*`, is twenty
209| five values grouped by the failure family they name.
210| 
211| | Code | What it signals |
212| | --- | --- |
213| | `AUTH_REQUIRED` | The call needs authentication that was not presented |
214| | `TOKEN_EXPIRED` | The presented token is no longer valid; refresh and retry |
215| | `PERMISSION_DENIED` | The authenticated principal lacks the required scope or permission |
216| | `PAYMENT_REQUIRED` | The account's billing state blocks the call |
217| | `RATE_LIMITED` | Too many requests; honor `retryAfterMs` before retrying |
218| | `NETWORK_UNREACHABLE` | The transport could not reach the daemon at all |
219| | `TIMEOUT` | The call started but did not finish in time |
220| | `CANCELLED` | The caller or runtime cancelled the call |
221| | `NOT_FOUND` | The addressed resource does not exist |
222| | `CONFLICT` | The mutation conflicts with current resource state |
223| | `SESSION_CLOSED` | The target session has already been closed |
224| | `NOT_INVOKABLE` | The gateway method exists but cannot be invoked over this path |
225| | `METHOD_NOT_FOUND` | No gateway method with that id exists |
226| | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | The input failed schema or contract validation |
227| | `AGENT_TIMEOUT` | A spawned agent exceeded its time budget |
228| | `AGENT_FAILED` | A spawned agent ended in failure |
229| | `TOOL_EXEC_FAILED` | A tool execution errored |
230| | `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` | A dependent service is down or refusing work |
231| | `CONTRACT_MISMATCH` | Client and daemon disagree about the contract shape |
232| | `PROTOCOL_ERROR` | The wire exchange itself violated the protocol |
233| | `INTERNAL_ERROR` | An unexpected internal failure with no more specific code |
234| | `ENGINE_CONFIGURATION_ERROR` | The platform was constructed or configured incorrectly |
235| | `ENGINE_CONTRACT_ERROR` | The platform detected a contract violation on its own side |
236| | `ENGINE_HTTP_STATUS_ERROR` | An HTTP status error carried no more specific mapping |
237| | `UNKNOWN` | Nothing more specific could be inferred |
238| 
239| ### Kind → representative code
240| 
241| The platform infers a representative canonical code for each `kind` (via `inferKind` and `inferCodeFromCategory`). The mapping is representative, not exhaustive. One `kind` may surface several codes (for example, `auth` covers `AUTH_REQUIRED`, `TOKEN_EXPIRED`, `PERMISSION_DENIED`, and `PAYMENT_REQUIRED`).
242| 
243| | `kind` | Representative `code` |
244| |--------|-----------------------|
245| | `auth` | `AUTH_REQUIRED` |
246| | `config` | `ENGINE_CONFIGURATION_ERROR` |
247| | `contract` | `CONTRACT_MISMATCH` |
248| | `network` | `NETWORK_UNREACHABLE` |
249| | `not-found` | `NOT_FOUND` |
250| | `protocol` | `PROTOCOL_ERROR` |
251| | `rate-limit` | `RATE_LIMITED` |
252| | `service` | `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` |
253| | `internal` | `INTERNAL_ERROR` |
254| | `tool` | `TOOL_EXEC_FAILED` |
255| | `validation` | `VALIDATION_FAILED` |
256| | `unknown` | `UNKNOWN` |
257| 
258| ---
259| 
260| ## Contract failure kinds and unmet criteria
261| 
262| > These are not `GoodVibesError` error kinds. They describe how a contract run by the contract runner ended or what its checks read, and can be confused for error kinds.
263| 
264| A contract that fails emits `CONTRACT_FAILED` on the `contracts` event domain with a `failureKind`, also stored as `Contract.failureKind` (`CONTRACT_FAILURE_KINDS`, `packages/engine/platform/src/events/contract.ts`):
265| 
266| | `failureKind` | Meaning |
267| |---|---|
268| | `transport` | A unit agent failed on a network error and its transport retries (`contract.transportRetryLimit`) were spent |
269| | `max_turns` | Declared on the wire with `turnLimit` and `turnLimitSource`. The runner does not end a contract with it: a unit agent that spends its turn budget is checked and woken with a nudge (the `agent-failed` check trigger) |
270| | `planning` | The planner agent failed: spawn error, cancel, bound exceeded, or a plan still unparseable after its repairs |
271| | `budget` | Declared on the wire. The runner does not end a contract with it: a unit held back by the contract's budget ceiling waits in `blocked` with the engine's reason |
272| | `owner-rejected` | The owner stopped the contract in reply to an escalation; recorded on the contract, which ends `cancelled` (`CONTRACT_CANCELLED`, reason "stopped by the owner") rather than failed |
273| | `judgment-unavailable` | Jev could not be asked or could not answer: no judgment port was installed, or the endpoint returned an error |
274| | `zombie` | At startup the contract's workstream snapshot or worktree was gone |
275| | `other` | Anything else; `reason` carries the message |
276| 
277| The contract's owner agent record fails with the same reason, so `AGENT_FAILED` for the owner carries it too.
278| 
279| Unmet acceptance criteria are not failures at all. A check that finds a criterion unmet emits `CONTRACT_CHECKED` with that criterion's `verdict: 'unmet'` and nudges the unit's agent (`CONTRACT_NUDGED`); the work continues until the criterion reads met or the owner decides. None of this is thrown or reaches the error handler or `PlatformObserver.onError`. See [Contract criteria](./contract-criteria.md).
280| 
281| ---
282| 
283| ## Typed error codes
284| 
285| Concrete `AppError` subclasses declare a **literal `code`** via `declare readonly code: '<LITERAL>'`, so narrowing to a specific subclass instance gives you that exact literal:
286| 
287| ```ts
288| export class ConfigError extends AppError {
289|   declare readonly code: 'CONFIG_ERROR';
290|   // ...
291| }
292| 
293| export class ProviderError extends AppError {
294|   declare readonly code: 'PROVIDER_ERROR';
295|   // ...
296| }
297| ```
298|

state.text:
299| > **`err.code` is not compiler-exhaustive.** A `switch (err.code)` with a `const _exhaustive: never = err.code` default does **not** type-check on a `GoodVibesError` or `AppError` value. `GoodVibesError.code` is typed `EngineErrorCode | (string & {})` and `AppError.code` is plain `string`. Both are wide string types, so the `never` assignment is a type error. The trick only compiles after you narrow to a finite, hand-built union of concrete subclasses, where each branch contributes its literal `code`:
300| 
301| ```ts
302| // Compiles only because `err` is narrowed to a finite subclass union first.
303| function handle(err: ConfigError | ProviderError): void {
304|   switch (err.code) {
305|     case 'CONFIG_ERROR':    /* ... */ break;
306|     case 'PROVIDER_ERROR':  /* ... */ break;
307|     default: {
308|       const _exhaustive: never = err.code;
309|       throw new Error('unhandled error code: ' + String(_exhaustive));
310|     }
311|   }
312| }
313| ```
314| 
315| Prefer `err.kind` for coarse handling (retry / auth / validation), and `err.code` when you need to disambiguate *which* concrete subclass a given `kind` came from.
316| 
317| ## Config errors and the AppError hierarchy
318| 
319| Two distinct error types relate to configuration; do not confuse them:
320| 
321| | Type | Code | Import subpath |
322| |------|------|----------------|
323| | `ConfigurationError` | `ENGINE_CONFIGURATION_ERROR` | `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/errors` |
324| | `ConfigError` | `CONFIG_ERROR` | `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/platform/types` |
325| 
326| `ConfigurationError` extends `GoodVibesError` directly and is thrown for invalid platform setup (category and kind `config`). `ConfigError` is an `AppError` subclass used by the platform/runtime layer.
327| 
328| `AppError` extends `GoodVibesError` and adds `statusCode`, `guidance`, `detail`, and `rawMessage`; its `code` is widened to plain `string`. The concrete subclasses ship under `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/platform/types`:
329| 
330| | Subclass | `code` | Recoverable |
331| |----------|--------|-------------|
332| | `ConfigError` | `CONFIG_ERROR` | No |
333| | `ProviderError` | `PROVIDER_ERROR` | When `statusCode` is in `RETRYABLE_STATUS_CODES` |
334| | `ToolError` | `TOOL_ERROR` | Yes |
335| | `AcpError` | `ACP_ERROR` | Yes |
336| | `PermissionError` | `PERMISSION_DENIED` | No |
337| | `RenderError` | `RENDER_ERROR` | Yes |
338| 
339| Subclass codes do **not** share one naming convention. `PERMISSION_DENIED` has no `_ERROR` suffix, while the others do.
340| 
341| ## Useful fields on every `GoodVibesError`
342| 
343| The class exposes 18 structured fields; `toJSON()` serializes them with `undefined` values omitted.
344| 
345| | Field | Type | Description |
346| |-------|------|-------------|
347| | `kind` | `EngineErrorKind` | Primary discriminant for switch/if handling. |
348| | `code` | `EngineErrorCode \| (string & {})` | Typed error code; canonical for platform errors, any string for caller-supplied codes. |
349| | `category` | `ErrorCategory` | Fine-grained classification (e.g. `authentication`, `rate_limit`). |
350| | `source` | `ErrorSource` | Where the error originated (`transport`, `contract`, `config`, etc.). |
351| | `recoverable` | `boolean` | Whether a retry is expected to succeed. |
352| | `status` | `number \| undefined` | HTTP status code if from a transport response. |
353| | `url` | `string \| undefined` | Request URL for transport failures. |
354| | `method` | `string \| undefined` | HTTP method for transport failures. |
355| | `body` | `unknown` | Parsed response body, when available. |
356| | `hint` | `string \| undefined` | Human-readable remediation hint from the server. |
357| | `provider` | `string \| undefined` | Provider name if the error originated in a provider call. |
358| | `operation` | `string \| undefined` | Operation/method name in progress when the error occurred. |
359| | `phase` | `string \| undefined` | Lifecycle phase in which the failure happened. |
360| | `requestId` | `string \| undefined` | Opaque ID for log correlation with the daemon. |
361| | `providerCode` | `string \| undefined` | Provider-specific error code. |
362| | `providerType` | `string \| undefined` | Provider type/family identifier. |
363| | `retryAfterMs` | `number \| undefined` | Milliseconds to wait before retrying (rate-limit). |
364| | `cause` | `unknown` | Original underlying error, preserved without loss. |
365|

1| # Expo integration
2| 
3| This is the **companion surface** for Expo (Hermes runtime). See [Published Surface Matrix](./surfaces.md).
4| 
5| Expo apps cannot run the full agentic surface (tool execution, LSP, MCP, workflows, daemon HTTP). Those require Bun. This guide covers auth, transport, realtime events, and error handling for the companion surface.
6| 
7| Use `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/expo` for Expo-managed React Native apps.
8| 
9| ```ts
10| import { createExpoGoodVibesPlatform } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/expo';
11| 
12| const platformClient = createExpoGoodVibesPlatform({
13|   baseUrl: 'https://goodvibes.example.com',
14|   authToken: token,
15| });
16| ```
17| 
18| ## Installation
19| 
20| ```bash
21| npm install @goodvibes-jev/engine
22| ```
23| 
24| See [Getting started](./getting-started.md#install) for the canonical install command and version. Token persistence uses the optional peer dependency [`expo-secure-store`](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/latest/sdk/securestore/) (`>=13.0.0`); install it only when you use `createExpoSecureTokenStore`.
25| 
26| ## Guidance
27| 
28| - prefer bearer tokens for Expo apps
29| - persist tokens with a secure `tokenStore` (see [Token storage](#token-storage)) rather than rolling a custom adapter
30| - use `platformClient.realtime.viaWebSocket()` for realtime. The Expo surface is WebSocket-only (no `viaSse()`), so the inherited `sseReconnect` option is a no-op
31| - reconnect on foreground/resume transitions
32| - wrap token access in a `tokenStore` or `getAuthToken` so reconnects do not keep stale tokens
33| 
34| ## Realtime
35| 
36| The Expo entrypoint wraps the React Native factory, so realtime is WebSocket-only: `platformClient.realtime` exposes `runtime()` and `viaWebSocket()` (there is no `viaSse()`). The factory applies the same defaults, which you can override through `GoodVibesPlatformOptions`:
37| 
38| - `realtime.webSocketReconnect`: `{ enabled: true, baseDelayMs: 500, maxDelayMs: 5000 }`
39| - `retry` (HTTP): `{ maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 250, maxDelayMs: 2000 }`
40| - `realtime.onError`: called when the realtime transport hits an unrecoverable error
41| 
42| The daemon authenticates the WebSocket upgrade request itself and answers 401
43| when it carries no `Authorization` header. Pass a header-attaching wrapper as
44| the `WebSocketImpl`, exactly as shown in
45| [React Native integration](./react-native-integration.md#realtime); the Expo
46| runtime's `WebSocket` supports the same headers option.
47| 
48| Scope a feed to a single session with `forSession` (re-exported from `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/expo`):
49| 
50| ```ts
51| import { createExpoGoodVibesPlatform, forSession } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/expo';
52| 
53| const sessionEvents = forSession(platformClient.realtime.viaWebSocket(AuthorizedWebSocket), sessionId);
54| sessionEvents.agents.on('AGENT_COMPLETED', (event) => console.log(event));
55| ```
56| 
57| ## Token storage
58| 
59| Pass a `tokenStore` to persist and rotate the bearer token. `tokenStore` is the highest-precedence auth option. It overrides both `getAuthToken` and the static `authToken`. Use `createExpoSecureTokenStore` (backed by `expo-secure-store`), exported from `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/expo`:
60| 
61| ```ts
62| import {
63|   createExpoGoodVibesPlatform,
64|   createExpoSecureTokenStore,
65| } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/expo';
66| 
67| const platformClient = createExpoGoodVibesPlatform({
68|   baseUrl: 'https://goodvibes.example.com',
69|   tokenStore: createExpoSecureTokenStore(),
70| });
71| ```
72| 
73| ## Typical Expo shape
74| 
75| - login or bootstrap the token once
76| - hydrate the platform from secure storage on app start
77| - load initial operator snapshots over HTTP
78| - subscribe to WebSocket runtime events for companion-app updates
79| - refresh read models after important events or foreground resumes
80| 
81| ## Error handling and observability
82| 
83| Error handling (the `GoodVibesError` taxonomy) and observability (`PlatformObserver` and `createConsoleObserver`) are identical to the React Native surface. The Expo factory wraps `createReactNativeGoodVibesPlatform`. See [Error handling](./react-native-integration.md#error-handling) and [Observability](./react-native-integration.md#observability) in the React Native guide.
84| 
85| ## Example
86| 
87| See [expo-quickstart.tsx](../examples/expo-quickstart.tsx).
88|

1| # React Native integration
2| 
3| This is the **companion surface** for React Native (Hermes). See [Published Surface Matrix](./surfaces.md).
4| 
5| React Native apps cannot run the full agentic surface (tool execution, LSP, MCP, workflows, daemon HTTP). Those require Bun. This guide covers auth, transport, realtime events, and error handling for the companion surface.
6| 
7| Use `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/react-native` for Android and iOS apps.
8| 
9| ```ts
10| import { createReactNativeGoodVibesPlatform } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/react-native';
11| 
12| const platformClient = createReactNativeGoodVibesPlatform({
13|   baseUrl: 'https://goodvibes.example.com',
14|   authToken: token,
15| });
16| ```
17| 
18| ## Installation
19| 
20| ```bash
21| npm install @goodvibes-jev/engine
22| ```
23| 
24| See [Getting started](./getting-started.md#install) for the canonical install command and version. For persistent secure token storage on bare React Native, also install the optional peer dependency [`react-native-keychain`](https://github.com/oblador/react-native-keychain) (`>=8.0.0`); it is only needed when you use `createIOSKeychainTokenStore` / `createAndroidKeystoreTokenStore`.
25| 
26| ## Realtime
27| 
28| The React Native realtime surface is WebSocket-only. `platformClient.realtime` exposes `runtime()` and `viaWebSocket()`. There is no `viaSse()`. SSE is unavailable on this surface, so the inherited `realtime.sseReconnect` option is a no-op here. Only `webSocketReconnect` applies.
29| 
30| The daemon authenticates the WebSocket upgrade request itself and answers 401
31| when it carries neither an `Authorization` header nor an operator session
32| cookie. The platform's in-band auth frame is only read after an authenticated
33| upgrade. React Native's `WebSocket` accepts a headers option, so pass a
34| wrapper as the `WebSocketImpl` that attaches the bearer token to the upgrade:
35| 
36| ```ts
37| const token = await SecureStore.getItemAsync('gv-token');
38| 
39| // React Native's WebSocket accepts (url, protocols, { headers }); the DOM
40| // types do not declare the third argument, hence the constructor cast.
41| type RNWebSocketCtor = new (
42|   url: string,
43|   protocols: string[],
44|   options: { headers: Record<string, string> },
45| ) => WebSocket;
46| 
47| const AuthorizedWebSocket = function (url: string | URL): WebSocket {
48|   return new (WebSocket as unknown as RNWebSocketCtor)(
49|     String(url),
50|     [],
51|     { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } },
52|   );
53| } as unknown as typeof WebSocket;
54| 
55| const events = platformClient.realtime.viaWebSocket(AuthorizedWebSocket);
56| const unsubscribe = events.agents.on('AGENT_COMPLETED', (event) => {
57|   console.log(event);
58| });
59| ```
60| 
61| The factory applies React-Native-tuned defaults that you can override through `GoodVibesPlatformOptions`:
62| 
63| - `realtime.webSocketReconnect`: `{ enabled: true, baseDelayMs: 500, maxDelayMs: 5000 }`
64| - `retry` (HTTP): `{ maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 250, maxDelayMs: 2000 }`
65| - `realtime.onError`: called when the realtime transport hits an unrecoverable error
66| 
67| To scope a feed to a single session, wrap it with `forSession` (re-exported from `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/react-native`):
68| 
69| ```ts
70| import { createReactNativeGoodVibesPlatform, forSession } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/react-native';
71| 
72| const sessionEvents = forSession(platformClient.realtime.viaWebSocket(AuthorizedWebSocket), sessionId);
73| sessionEvents.agents.on('AGENT_COMPLETED', (event) => console.log(event));
74| ```
75| 
76| ## Token storage
77| 
78| Pass a `tokenStore` to persist and rotate the bearer token. `tokenStore` is the highest-precedence auth option. It overrides both `getAuthToken` and the static `authToken`. Use `createIOSKeychainTokenStore` (iOS Keychain) or `createAndroidKeystoreTokenStore` (Android Keystore), both exported from `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/react-native`, rather than rolling a custom `GoodVibesTokenStore`:
79| 
80| ```ts
81| import {
82|   createReactNativeGoodVibesPlatform,
83|   createIOSKeychainTokenStore,
84| } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/react-native';
85| 
86| const platformClient = createReactNativeGoodVibesPlatform({
87|   baseUrl: 'https://goodvibes.example.com',
88|   tokenStore: createIOSKeychainTokenStore(),
89| });
90| ```
91| 
92| On Android, use `createAndroidKeystoreTokenStore()` in place of the Keychain store.
93| 
94| ## Error handling
95| 
96| All platform errors extend `GoodVibesError`. See [Error Kinds](./error-kinds.md) for the full taxonomy.
97| 
98| ```ts
99| import { GoodVibesError } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/errors';
100| 
101| try {
102|   await platformClient.operator.control.snapshot();
103| } catch (err) {
104|   if (err instanceof GoodVibesError) {
105|     switch (err.kind) {
106|       case 'auth':
107|         // token expired, refresh and retry
108|         break;
109|       case 'network':
110|         // transport failure, reconnect or surface to user
111|         break;
112|       case 'service':
113|         // daemon or upstream service returned 5xx, log and degrade gracefully
114|         break;
115|       case 'protocol':
116|         // client and daemon disagreed about the wire contract
117|         break;
118|       default:
119|         throw err;
120|     }
121|   }
122| }
123| ```
124| 
125| ## Observability
126| 
127| `PlatformObserver` and `createConsoleObserver` work from React Native exactly like from the full surface. They are imported from `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform` root, which is companion-safe. See [Observability](./observability.md) for the full observer API.
128| 
129| ```ts
130| import { createConsoleObserver } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform';
131| 
132| const platformClient = createReactNativeGoodVibesPlatform({
133|   baseUrl: 'https://goodvibes.example.com',
134|   authToken: token,
135|   observer: createConsoleObserver(),
136| });
137| ```
138| 
139| ## Example
140| 
141| See [react-native-quickstart.ts](../examples/react-native-quickstart.ts) for a runnable end-to-end example.
142| 
143| ## Notes
144| 
145| - `fetch` can come from the React Native runtime or be injected explicitly.
146| - `WebSocket` can come from the runtime or be passed through `WebSocketImpl`.
147| - The React Native entrypoint is WebSocket-only; SSE (`viaSse`) is not exposed and `sseReconnect` is a no-op.
148| - Provide a token store or `getAuthToken` when token state can rotate during the app session. See [Token storage](#token-storage).
149| - Reconnect after foreground/resume and network transitions.
150| - Use HTTP for snapshots/mutations and WebSocket for live updates.
151| - For Expo-managed apps, use [expo-integration.md](./expo-integration.md).
152| - For native Kotlin or Swift apps, use [android-integration.md](./android-integration.md) and [ios-integration.md](./ios-integration.md).
153|

1| # Web UI integration
2| 
3| This is the **companion surface** for web UI applications (browser runtime). See [Runtime Surfaces](./surfaces.md).
4| 
5| Web UI apps cannot run the full agentic surface (tool execution, LSP, MCP, workflows, daemon HTTP). Those require Bun. This guide covers web-UI-specific patterns: entrypoint selection, companion chat, attachments, and voice playback. The shared browser foundation, auth, transport, realtime, error handling, and observability, lives in [Browser integration](./browser-integration.md).
6| 
7| Use the narrowest browser entrypoint that matches the app. A normal GoodVibes
8| WebUI that presents the base knowledge/wiki system should use
9| `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/knowledge`; it contains base knowledge routes,
10| shared session/auth/provider routes, and realtime domains without loading Home
11| Assistant Home Graph route metadata. Use `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser` only
12| when the app intentionally needs the complete operator route contract.
13| 
14| ```ts
15| import { createBrowserKnowledgePlatform } from '@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/knowledge';
16| 
17| const platformClient = createBrowserKnowledgePlatform({
18|   baseUrl: 'https://goodvibes.example.com',
19| });
20| ```
21| 
22| ## Deployment topology: same-origin vs cross-origin
23| 
24| The daemon can reach a browser two ways. Both are opt-in and off by default; the
25| daemon stays loopback-only until you enable one.
26| 
27| **Same-origin bundle serving (recommended).** Set `controlPlane.webui.serve` on and
28| point `controlPlane.webui.bundleDir` at the built web UI directory (`index.html` +
29| `assets/`). The daemon then serves the bundle at `/` from its own origin, so the
30| browser's same-origin policy is a non-issue. Bundle and API share one origin. Static
31| assets carry correct content types and caching (hashed `assets/*` immutable, the shell
32| `no-cache`), and unknown navigation routes fall back to `index.html` (SPA). The daemon's
33| own routes always keep precedence over the bundle: every `/api/*` path, `/login`,
34| `/webhook/*`, `/task`, the OpenAI-compatible prefix, and every other top-level path
35| segment any operator method advertises (for example `/status` and `/config`) is
36| dispatched to the API and never served as a file, so an SPA fallback can never shadow
37| a liveness probe or an admin read with the HTML shell. The bundle is public; the
38| app still token-authenticates every API call.
39| 
40| For cross-machine reach, front the single daemon origin with `tailscale serve` over
41| HTTPS: bundle + API arrive same-origin on the Tailscale hostname with zero CORS. This
42| is the supported remote path.
43| 
44| **Cross-origin (dev or separate host).** When the UI is served from a different origin,
45| the Vite dev server on `http://localhost:5173`, or a deliberately separate static host
46| set `controlPlane.cors.enabled` on and list the exact browser origins in
47| `controlPlane.cors.allowedOrigins` (comma-separated). The daemon then answers OPTIONS
48| preflight and emits `Access-Control-Allow-*` only for those origins, never a wildcard,
49| credentials allowlist-gated, `Authorization` allowed so the bearer-token flow works.
50| A non-allowlisted origin is refused honestly (403 preflight, no allow-origin header).
51| CORS controls only which origin may read a response; it does not change any route's auth
52| or admin scoping.
53| 
54| ## Recommended model
55| 
56| For a browser-based web UI:
57| - use the narrowest scoped browser entrypoint
58| - prefer same-origin cookie-backed auth when hosting the UI with the daemon
59| - use `platformClient.realtime.viaSse()` for dashboards and live status panes
60| - use `platformClient.knowledge.*` or `platformClient.operator.invoke(...)` for the base knowledge/wiki methods exposed by the scoped entrypoint
61| - use `platformClient.chat.*` for standalone companion chat sessions
62| - use `platformClient.operator.invoke('control.snapshot', {})` for shared control-plane state
63| - treat realtime as live update flow, not as the only source of truth
64| 
65| ## Choosing browser entrypoints
66| 
67| `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/knowledge` is the default for the base GoodVibes
68| WebUI. `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/homeassistant` is for Home Assistant
69| panels and includes Home Graph routes without pulling the base knowledge/wiki
70| route table. `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/agent` (via `createBrowserAgentPlatform`)
71| scopes to the GoodVibes Agent surface: the agent's own knowledge/wiki space
72| served under `/api/goodvibes-agent/knowledge`, plus work-plan, artifact, and
73| companion-chat routes. `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser` and
74| `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/web` remain full all-method browser clients for
75| applications that need the entire operator contract.
76| 
77| See [public-surface.md](./public-surface.md) for the full entry-point reference.
78| 
79| ## Typical web UI pattern
80| 
81| 1. Load an initial snapshot with operator APIs.
82| 2. Subscribe to runtime events or telemetry streams.
83| 3. Refresh affected read models when key events arrive.
84| 4. Keep mutation calls on HTTP even when realtime is enabled.
85| 
86| ## Companion chat
87| 
88| Use `platformClient.chat` from `@goodvibes-jev/engine/platform/browser/knowledge` for standalone
89| browser chat. These sessions are separate from operator task sessions and do
90| not call `sessions.followUp`.
91| 
92| ```ts
93| const created = await platformClient.chat.sessions.create({
94|   title: 'WebUI chat',
95|   provider: 'openai-subscriber',
96|   model: 'gpt-5.5',
97| });
98| 
99| await platformClient.chat.events.stream(created.sessionId, {
100|   onEvent(eventName, payload) {
101|     // companion-chat.turn.delta / companion-chat.turn.completed / companion-chat.turn.error
102|   },
103| });
104| 
105| await platformClient.chat.messages.create(created.sessionId, {
106|   body: 'Hello',
107| });
108| ```
109| 
110| `provider` is the selected runtime provider row id from the model catalog, for
111| example `openai-subscriber`. `model` is the selected model id for that provider
112| row, for example `gpt-5.5`. When a runtime provider is an alias for a catalog
113| provider, the daemon also accepts the provider-qualified registry key as
114| `model`, such as `openai:gpt-5.5`, as long as `provider` remains the selected
115| runtime provider row id.
116| 
117| Use `platformClient.chat.sessions.list()` for the chat sidebar and
118| `platformClient.chat.sessions.update(sessionId, { provider, model })` when a user changes
119| the model for an existing companion-chat session. Do not send provider/model on
120| `messages.create`; message creation uses the session's stored route.
121| 
122| ### Chat attachments
123| 
124| Companion chat attachments are artifact-backed. Upload the file to the daemon
125| artifact store first, then reference the returned artifact id when creating the
126| chat message. Do not encode files in message metadata and do not create local
127| attachment-only state in the WebUI.
128| 
129| ```ts
130| const uploaded = await platformClient.artifacts.create({
131|   filename: file.name,
132|   mimeType: file.type || 'application/octet-stream',
133|   dataBase64: await fileToBase64(file),
134|   metadata: { surface: 'webui' },
135| });
136| 
137| await platformClient.chat.messages.create(created.sessionId, {
138|   body: 'Use this file in your answer.',
139|   attachments: [
140|     {
141|       artifactId: uploaded.artifact.id,
142|       label: file.name,
143|     },
144|   ],
145| });
146| ```
147| 
148| `messages.create` accepts text-only, attachment-only, and text-plus-attachment
149| messages, up to 8 attachments per message. Message history and
150| `companion-chat.turn.started` events include the resolved attachment descriptors.
151| 
152| What the daemon does with an attachment depends on its size and MIME type. A text
153| artifact (`text/*`, `application/json`, `application/xml`, `application/yaml`, or
154| `text/csv`) up to 200 KB is read back and inlined into the provider prompt as plain
155| text. An image artifact (`image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/gif`, or `image/webp`) up
156| to 20 MB is base64-encoded and passed as multimodal image content. Everything else,
157| and anything over those size limits, stays a durable artifact reference: the model
158| sees only a text summary listing the attachment's name, MIME type, and size, not
159| its contents.
160|

162| 
163| `POST /api/voice/tts/stream` returns raw audio bytes as a stream (see
